description:
Paul Silas Moos leads the student rocketry association HybridLaunch and studies physics with a focus on technologies for space applications. He received the 2026 JEP! Youth Engagement Award for his work as an engineering mentor.

Stephanie Käs is a PhD researcher, specialising in astronaut movement analysis. She also serves as a science communicator for HybridLaunch and is a 2026 Zonta Women in STEM Award recipient for District 29.
summary:
We developed Moon Mission, a cooperative board game designed for children aged 9–12. Players operate a lunar base and explore the surrounding landscape, working together to collect a sample from a distant crater and bring it safely home. Along the way, they manage water, oxygen, and power while responding to unexpected events and environmental hazards.
Our project addresses the challenge of making space exploration understandable and engaging for children. Information about real missions is embedded in the game materials, while a parent information sheet supports discussion beyond the game. An accompanying data analysis sheet explains the research behind our simplified resource model.
By combining hands-on play, teamwork, and scientific information, we aim to help children develop a realistic understanding of space exploration—and discover why preparation, limited resources, and cooperation matter to a successful mission.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS

Two to four children jointly control a four-person crew, sharing four actions each game day between maintaining the base, managing water and oxygen supplies, charging batteries, and exploring a route revealed through terrain tiles and discovery cards. To complete the mission, they must check the life-support systems, activate a communications relay, and collect and seal a crater sample in three steps before returning it to the base within eight game days. Alternating light and darkness affect solar charging, while radiation and meteoroid warning markers move after every action, encouraging players to plan their movements, seek protection, and preserve enough energy for the journey home.

The game creates opportunities for face-to-face interaction, shared decisions, and cooperative problem-solving. Children work towards a common goal, reflecting the teamwork required in space missions. The parent information sheet gives adults background knowledge and conversation prompts, connecting the experience across generations. Short facts on the game materials allow children to encounter information about real missions naturally as they play. Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity while building an understanding of the practical challenges behind exploration.


BUILDING THE GAME

We used Python to model resources and simulate games, and HTML to present simulation replays and results. Codex supported information gathering, web searches, coding, and the development of simulations. Our research also drew on books about lunar and Mars exploration accessed through university online libraries, alongside resources such as the Biosphere 2 website. We used ChatGPT for image generation and Gemini for video creation, then crafted the physical prototype from paper.

Our original concept was a Mars base with plants and more extensive self-sufficiency systems. We shifted to a lunar mission because we considered it a more realistic near-term setting, connected to exploration that children might follow within their own lifetimes. Bringing a physical board game to a coding challenge was central to our creative approach: software supported the research, development, and testing of an experience played together around a table.

Our main design challenge was balancing realism, accessibility, and fun. We checked resource data but translated quantities and technical units into manageable counters and simple decisions. We chose cooperation because mission success depends on collective effort, and worked to keep essential maintenance from becoming repetitive. With Codex’s help, we ran thousands of simulated games to investigate resource shortages, strategies, and repetitive action patterns—far more rounds than we could play ourselves over one weekend. These simulations supported mechanical testing; testing with children is still needed to assess enjoyment, clarity, and playing time.



OUR VISION
As a young couple, we hope to share our enthusiasm for space, knowledge, and practical engineering skills with our future children—often through activities without screens. We created this cooperative game to bring children and adults together for storytelling, discussion, discovery, and shared problem-solving.

Future versions could introduce deeper scientific detail and more flexible exploration, with movement costing each astronaut working time, inspired by Legends of Andor. A digital adaptation could support more detailed resource calculations, but we value children doing the maths themselves and understanding their decisions through hands-on play.
